title: 🏗️ Heights and Distances — Multi-Step Problems
hook: A pilot needs to calculate the landing distance. A surveyor measures a mountain's height from two different spots. These real-world problems use TWO right triangles and the magic of trigonometry!
explanation:
Two-triangle problems: These are the most common advanced questions. You get two angle measurements from different positions.

1
From A
tan α = h / (d + BC) … where BC = distance from B to tower base
2
From B
tan β = h / BC
3
Two equations, two unknowns
Solve simultaneously for h
💡 Tip: The key trick: express the horizontal distance in terms of h using one equation, then substitute into the other.
⚠️ Tip: Always check if the observer is on the same side or opposite sides of the tower — the equations differ!
worked_example:
Example: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points at distances a and b from the base, in the same straight line, are complementary (sum to 90°). Prove: height = √(ab).

1
Let angles be θ and (90°−θ)
Tower height = h
2
From distance a
tan θ = h/a → h = a·tan θ …(1)
3
From distance b
tan(90°−θ) = h/b → cot θ = h/b → h = b·cot θ …(2)
4
Multiply (1) and (2)
h² = ab·tan θ·cot θ = ab·1 = ab
5
Therefore
h = √(ab) ∎

try_this.question: The angle of elevation of a cloud from a point 60 m above a lake is 30° and the angle of depression of its reflection in the lake is 60°. Find the height of the cloud above the lake.
try_this.hint: Let cloud be h above lake. Observer is 60 m above lake. Cloud reflection is h below lake surface. Use tan 30° and tan 60° with the same horizontal distance.
try_this.answer: Let cloud height above lake = H. Observer is 60 m above lake. tan 30° = (H−60)/d → d = (H−60)√3. tan 60° = (H+60)/d → d = (H+60)/√3. So (H−60)√3 = (H+60)/√3. 3(H−60) = H+60. 3H−180 = H+60. 2H = 240. H = 120 m.

fun_fact: The Great Trigonometrical Survey of India (1802-1871) used these exact techniques to measure the height of Mount Everest — getting within 8 meters of the modern measurement using only theodolites and trigonometry!
